events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Maya proposes Maya, Elena. I know I am a Loyal Servant and therefore Good, so I include myself to secure at least one Good member. With no other private information, I choose Elena as the second player for Mission 1.

Maya’s self-inclusion makes sense, but Elena is an unknown from my perspective. I’d prefer a team of Maya and Kenji, since I know I’m Good. That said, there’s little public evidence to distinguish these options yet.

I understand Kenji’s point that a team of Maya and Kenji would give Kenji certainty about one member, but from my perspective I also know I am a Loyal Servant, so my self-inclusion is based on public reasoning available to me. I do not have private information clearing Elena or Kenji. For Mission 1, I am keeping the proposal as Maya and Elena unless discussion gives a concrete public reason to revise. I want to hear whether others see specific risks in Elena or a better case for another second member, but I will not treat Kenji’s self-claim as verified.

I support Maya's proposal of Maya and Elena for Mission 1. Maya's reasoning is sound: with no public information to distinguish any of us, anchoring the team on a player who has explained their logic openly is a reasonable starting point, and a two-player team keeps our exposure minimal if anything goes wrong. Kenji, I hear your preference for a team including yourself, and I understand the instinct, but I'd caution everyone against treating self-declarations of being Good as evidence. Any player can make that claim, and at this stage it tells us nothing about the actual composition of the game. For what it's worth, I have no concerns about this specific pairing, and I see no concrete reason to swap anyone in or out. My priority on the first mission is to get a clean result and start building a picture of where the Fail cards come from, if any appear. Keeping the team simple and voting honestly on it gives us more information than churning through alternative proposals with nothing to base them on. I'd rather save our rejections for cases where we have actual evidence. I'm ready to vote yes on Maya and Elena as proposed.

I've already stated my support for the Maya and Elena pairing, and nothing in the discussion so far has changed my view. Maya has explained her reasoning transparently: she includes herself based on her own role knowledge, and the second slot is essentially arbitrary given that no one has produced a single piece of public evidence against any candidate. Kenji's counter-proposal rests entirely on his own self-declaration of being Good, which as I noted earlier carries no evidentiary weight — every player in this game could make the identical claim. If we start swapping team members based on unverified self-claims alone, we create a precedent where any confident declaration can hijack team selection, and that helps Evil far more than it helps us. My earlier point stands: the value of a first mission is a clean signal. If this team fails, we learn Fail cards came from within Maya and Elena, which is a strong starting point for narrowing suspects. If it succeeds, we've banked a mission and eliminated two players from suspicion, at least partially. Either outcome is informative. Churning to an alternative proposal now, with zero evidence to distinguish anyone, gives us strictly less information and risks burning rejections we may need later. One thing I would add: I'd encourage everyone to watch how players argue rather than what they claim about themselves. Confidence without substance, or pressure to include specific people without reasons, is worth noting as the game develops. On the merits of this specific proposal, I see no risk that justifies a revision, and I'm ready to vote yes on Maya and Elena as proposed.

A successful mission would be useful, but it would not clear Maya or Elena: an Evil player can play Success. I still prefer a team including me, and I would support Kenji and Isha as an alternative. That preference is based on my own perspective, not a public claim that Isha is cleared.

Kenji's latest message actually strengthens the case for keeping this team exactly as it is. Notice what he just conceded: a successful mission clears no one, because Evil can play Success. Fine — but that cuts both ways. It means there is no cost to approving a reasonable first team and letting it go on a mission, and there is no benefit to churn. Yet he still insists on a team including himself, now floating Kenji and Isha as an alternative. So let's look at the pattern. Kenji's only stated qualification for membership is his own claim that he is Good — a claim he has now repeated three times while offering nothing else. No reasoning about team composition, no caution about information gathering, just a persistent push to insert himself. That is precisely the kind of behavior I flagged earlier: pressure to include specific people without reasons. On a five-player board, a first mission team of two is a pure information-gathering play, and the players most eager to be on it deserve the most scrutiny from us later. I will not vote for a revision built on unverified self-declaration, and I'd urge Maya to hold firm. The Maya and Elena proposal is transparent, its logic is stated publicly, and either outcome of the mission gives us real signal. Rejecting a clean proposal now to hand a slot to the loudest self-advocate would be the worst of both worlds: we'd burn rejection capital and muddy the information we get. Keep the team as proposed, vote it up, and let's start building the picture from the actual mission result.

Elena, saying there is no cost to approving this team overlooks the possibility that it fails. My preference for including myself is based on my own knowledge, just as Maya's self-inclusion is based on hers; it is not public proof for anyone else. Elena's insistence that this team is effectively risk-free goes beyond what we know. Maya, would you reconsider the second slot and propose Maya and Kenji instead?

Kenji, I have considered your request to replace Elena with you. I understand that from your perspective a team including you would give you certainty about one member, just as my self-inclusion gives me certainty about myself. But that is a private perspective, not public evidence for the rest of us. I do not have private information clearing Elena or you, and I do not treat either player's self-claim as verified. Elena's support for the proposal also does not clear her; it is simply one line of argument. What matters now is whether there is a concrete public reason to swap the second slot. I have not heard one. Your preference is understandable, but it rests on the same kind of self-knowledge I used when proposing myself, and it does not distinguish you from Elena in a way others can evaluate. For Mission 1, I am keeping the proposal as Maya and Elena. A two-player team is a limited information-gathering play, and either result gives us something to work from. I am not accusing you of being Evil for advocating for yourself; I am saying that advocacy is not enough to justify revising a transparent first proposal. I will keep the team as proposed.

I agree with Maya that without concrete information, churning through proposals based purely on self-claims does not help Good. Kenji's desire to be on the team is understandable from his own viewpoint, but it offers no verifiable evidence to the rest of us. At the same time, Elena spending all three of her speaking turns aggressively disputing Kenji's push was noticeable, though it is understandable for a nominated player to advocate for their team. On the first proposal of Mission 1, Maya and Elena is a clean test that gives us clear accountability. Isha, you have not weighed in yet. Where do you stand on approving Maya and Elena, and how do you view the back-and-forth between Kenji and Elena?

Zara, thanks for asking. I will approve Maya and Elena as proposed. Mission 1 is a two-player test, and rejecting a transparent proposal with no public evidence would only burn a rejection. I am not endorsing Kenji's self-claim, and nothing we have heard gives a concrete reason to swap him in. On the back-and-forth, I agree that Elena spent much of her time defending the team against Kenji, and that intensity is worth remembering. It is not proof of anything, but it is a pattern to track alongside how players respond when pressed. Maya's reasoning has been consistent and I have no objection to it. Let's see the mission result and then judge who stayed consistent.

I still support Maya and Elena as the Mission 1 team. Neither a self-claim of being Good nor a push to swap in a particular player is public evidence, so I see no concrete reason to reject a transparent proposal. Elena's defense of the team has been forceful, but intensity alone is not grounds for rejection. I would rather we vote honestly on this team, see the mission result, and then judge each player on how their reasoning holds up over time.

My final word before the vote: I approve Maya and Elena. Mission 1 is a two-player test, and no one has offered public evidence that justifies a rejection. Maya has explained her reasoning consistently, and Elena has defended the team in a way that is open to scrutiny, which we can judge after the mission result. Self-claims of being Good are not evidence for anyone, so I will weigh each player on how their reasoning holds up over time. I will vote yes on Maya and Elena.

Maya confirms Maya, Elena. No concrete public evidence has emerged to justify replacing Elena, and my own reasoning for including myself remains unchanged. A two-player first mission is a clean information-gathering test, so I will keep the proposal as Maya and Elena.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Elena proposes Elena, Maya, Zara. Mission 1's Maya–Elena team succeeded with no fail cards, so I want to build on that core rather than churn the roster. I propose Elena, Maya, and Zara. Maya has proven herself through a clean Mission 1 result and transparent reasoning throughout the first discussion. Zara has been measured and constructive, offering a balanced read on the Kenji–Elena exchange without pressure tactics. I exclude Isha and Kenji because Kenji spent the entire first discussion pushing to insert himself into the team based solely on unverified self-claims, and Isha, while supportive of the final team, showed no particular resistance to that pressure — neither has done anything to earn a slot over the players who have reasoned openly. This team keeps our exposure limited while preserving continuity of the players whose arguments have held up under scrutiny.

Mission 1 succeeded, but that does not prove Maya or Elena is Good: an Evil player could have played Success. Elena also says Isha showed no resistance to my pressure, but Isha explicitly supported the original team and rejected my case for a swap. That exclusion rationale misrepresents the discussion.

I would prefer a team including me, since I know my own alignment, though I recognize that is not evidence for anyone else. Maya, do you agree that Elena's description of Isha's position is inaccurate, and does that affect your view of this team?

Kenji, yes: Isha did support the original Maya–Elena team and explicitly said there was no concrete reason to swap. Elena’s claim that Isha showed no particular resistance to your pressure is therefore inaccurate. That does not prove Elena is Evil, but it weakens the exclusion rationale she gave and matters more on a three-player Mission 2. I know my own alignment is Good; Mission 1’s success is only weak evidence for Elena, since an Evil player can play Success. Zara has been measured, but I have no public proof clearing her. I am not comfortable treating this mischaracterization as a minor slip without clarification. Elena, can you correct or explain why you described Isha’s position that way before we vote?

Maya and Kenji are right on the specific point, and I will correct the record plainly: Isha did explicitly support the Maya–Elena team in Mission 1's discussion and voted yes. My statement that Isha showed 'no particular resistance' to Kenji's pressure was an overstatement, and I withdraw it. Isha's actual position was clearer support than I credited. That was my error in summarizing, and Maya is also right that it does not by itself prove anything about anyone's alignment — it weakens one line of my exclusion rationale, and I acknowledge that directly rather than dressing it up as a minor slip.

With that corrected, let me restate why I am keeping this team as proposed. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards, and Maya's reasoning throughout has been consistent and transparent. Zara's contribution was measured: she flagged Elena's intensity — mine — as worth tracking while still concluding the proposal was a clean test. That is exactly the kind of even-handed reading Good needs. The team of Elena, Maya, and Zara preserves continuity from a proven result while adding one fresh player, and it does so on publicly stated reasoning rather than private self-claims.

What I will not do is revise the team in response to Kenji's persistent push to be included. This is now the second consecutive discussion in which Kenji's core argument is 'I know my own alignment.' Maya correctly identified in Mission 1 that this is a private perspective, not public evidence, and nothing has changed. He has also, notably, now attempted to use a correction about Isha's characterization as leverage to unsettle a team that does not include him — that is a pattern of pressure without substance, and I would ask everyone to weigh it when voting.

To be clear about the standard I am holding myself to: I made a mischaracterization, it was caught, and I have corrected it on the record. That is how reasoning should work in this game. I am comfortable being judged on my consistency, including this correction.

The choice before us is straightforward. Approve a three-player team built from a successful Mission 1 core and a balanced third member, or churn the roster to satisfy an unsubstantiated self-advocacy campaign. I am keeping Elena, Maya, and Zara as proposed, and I will vote yes. If the mission fails, we will have a precise and damning signal about where a fail card came from, and I will accept full scrutiny as a team member.

Maya, with the mischaracterization corrected on the record, does that resolve your concern, and will you support this team as proposed?

Elena, yes — your correction resolves the specific factual concern about Isha. You withdrew the inaccurate description of Isha’s Mission 1 position, and that matters more than dressing it up as a minor slip. It does not clear you, and Mission 1’s success is only weak evidence for you because an Evil player could have played Success. Zara also remains unverified from my perspective. But I do not see a concrete public reason to reject this three-player team now. The proposal preserves the successful Maya–Elena core and adds one fresh player, and either mission result gives us useful signal: if it fails, the Fail came from Elena, Maya, or Zara; if it succeeds, that is still not full clearance for anyone. Kenji’s repeated self-claim is not public evidence, and I will not revise the team merely to satisfy self-advocacy. I will vote yes on Elena, Maya, and Zara as proposed.

Elena, thank you for correcting the record. But your choice of Zara over Isha still rests on a thin distinction: Isha also supported the original team and gave a measured assessment of the discussion. Mission 1's success is useful, but it does not prove its members are Good.

I would prefer a team including me from my own perspective; if that is not persuasive to others, I think Isha deserves equal consideration for Zara's slot. Elena, what specifically makes Zara a stronger choice than Isha now that you've withdrawn your earlier characterization?

Kenji, you asked what specifically makes Zara a stronger choice than Isha now that I've withdrawn my mischaracterization. Here is the answer on the public record. Zara's contribution in Mission 1 was independent and evaluative. She agreed with Maya's position on its merits, but she also flagged my own intensity in defending the team as a pattern worth tracking. That is exactly the kind of judgment Good needs on a mission team: she did not rubber-stamp the nominated players, she applied the same standard to me as to you, and she reached a conclusion based on reasoning rather than alignment with whoever spoke last or loudest. She also did the useful work of drawing Isha into the discussion when Isha had not yet spoken. Isha's contributions, by contrast, were confirmatory. All three of Isha's turns restated the same position — approve the transparent proposal, no concrete reason to swap — without adding analysis, without pressing either side, and without flagging anything for the group to track later. That is not an accusation of anything; it is a distinction in demonstrated judgment. On a three-player mission, I want the seat to go to the player who has shown she evaluates rather than echoes, and that is Zara. Now, to the broader point you keep raising: you are right that Mission 1's success does not clear Maya or Elena, because an Evil player can play Success. I have never claimed otherwise, and I said explicitly that a fail result on this mission would give a precise signal precisely because no one is cleared. That cuts against your argument, not for it. If mission results prove nothing, then there is no informational advantage to reshuffling the roster to include you — only the same self-claim, repeated across three discussions now, that everyone else has consistently declined to treat as evidence. You also say Isha deserves equal consideration for Zara's slot. Fine — but the person who earned a slot through demonstrated independent judgment should not lose it to satisfy an unverified preference, whether yours or relayed on Isha's behalf. I am keeping Elena, Maya, and Zara as proposed, and I will vote yes. Kenji, one direct question: if this team is approved, will you support it on the mission rather than positioning yourself to argue afterward that the result proves nothing?

Elena, I hope the mission succeeds if this team is approved, but I will not pretend a Success would prove everyone on it is Good. A Fail would be serious evidence against the team; a Success would be useful but not conclusive.

Your comparison of Zara and Isha also overlooks that Isha explicitly said your intensity was a pattern worth tracking. And your proposal said Maya had “proven herself,” even though you now acknowledge that Mission 1 did not clear her. Those inconsistencies make me less confident in your selection process. I will vote against Elena, Maya, and Zara.

I appreciate Elena putting me on this proposal. From my own perspective, I know I am Good, so my presence secures at least one Loyal Servant on the team.

Regarding the debate so far: Kenji is correct that Mission 1's success does not definitively clear Maya or Elena, as an Evil player can certainly play Success to build trust. However, absent any concrete evidence of foul play, testing the core of a successful mission alongside a fresh player is our most reliable path forward. Elena promptly retracted her mischaracterization of Isha when challenged, which demonstrates accountability rather than evasiveness.

Kenji, while your scrutiny of wording has kept the discussion sharp, repeatedly rejecting proposals simply because you are excluded—while offering only private role knowledge as justification—does not give the table a viable reason to churn.

I intend to vote yes on Elena, Maya, and Zara. Isha, since your position and demeanor in Mission 1 were heavily analyzed by both Elena and Kenji, I would like to hear your perspective directly: do you support this team, and how do you view Elena’s rationale for choosing me over you?

Zara, to your question: I support Elena, Maya, and Zara as the Mission 2 team and will vote yes. I am not on it, and with one successful mission behind this group, rejecting it now would spend a rejection without new evidence. On Elena's rationale, my exclusion was not decided on evidence. She first said I showed no particular resistance to Kenji's pressure, which she has now withdrawn. She then ranked Zara above me by calling my turns confirmatory, but I had supported the transparent Mission 1 proposal and restated it when challenged, and that is not a reason to rank players. Her Mission 2 proposal also called Maya proven after a Mission 1 success that she herself says clears no one, which is an overreach. I do not treat Kenji's self-claim as evidence, and I am not asking anyone to take my side on that basis. My view is simply that this team is approvable and we should judge it by the mission result. Elena, you credited Zara with independent judgment for flagging your intensity, but you called my position confirmatory for doing the same kind of work. What is the difference, in your view, between Zara's contribution and mine?

Isha, you asked what the difference is between Zara's contribution and yours, and I will answer precisely. Zara did three things in Mission 1 that you did not do. First, she evaluated the nominated players against a stated standard rather than simply endorsing a transparent process — she explicitly flagged my intensity as a pattern worth tracking while still concluding the proposal was a clean test. Second, she drew you into the discussion when you had not yet spoken, doing work that grew the record rather than restating it. Third, she resisted Kenji's push without relying on anyone's self-claims in either direction. Your three turns, by contrast, each restated the same conclusion — approve the team, no concrete reason to swap — and notably, your criticism of my intensity only surfaced in Mission 2, after I excluded you from the proposal. In Mission 1, when the intensity was actually happening, your turns raised no such concern. That timing is worth the table's attention: a concern raised for the first time after one is excluded reads as a grievance, not an observation.

On your other points: yes, my draft called Maya 'proven,' and that was loose phrasing — Mission 1's success is weak evidence, not clearance, as I said explicitly in the same discussion. Kenji is right that the word overreached, and I own that. But notice the structure of the pressure you and Kenji are applying in tandem. Kenji has pushed for his own inclusion across two consecutive discussions on nothing but a private self-claim, and now that his push has failed, you arrive to relitigate the same exclusion with the same lack of any concrete alternative. Neither of you has proposed a roster, identified a risk in Maya or Zara, or offered a reason to churn beyond 'the process was imperfect.' An imperfect process with a transparent rationale and a corrected record is still better than churn with no rationale at all.

Isha, so here is my direct question to you: setting aside your grievance about the slot, do you believe Maya or Zara specifically should not be on this mission — and if so, on what concrete evidence other than the fact that you and Kenji are the two players left off it? If your answer is again that the team is merely 'approvable' and we should wait for results, then we agree on the outcome, and the discussion is settled. I am keeping Elena, Maya, and Zara as proposed and voting yes. If this mission fails, the Fail came from one of the three of us, and I will accept full scrutiny — that is the precise accountability a three-player team provides, and I asked for it myself.

Elena, my Mission 1 record contradicts your timing claim. In my turns e13 and e14, before any Mission 2 roster existed, I said Elena's defense of the team had been forceful and was a pattern to track. So that concern was not raised after my exclusion. I still approve Elena, Maya, and Zara as the Mission 2 team. I am not claiming Maya or Zara should be excluded, and I have no concrete evidence against either of them. My questions were about your selection rationale, not about the players themselves. Your Mission 2 draft called Maya proven, which you have now acknowledged was loose, and I accept your correction about Isha's position. I will judge this team by its result. Zara, you called Kenji's scrutiny sharp. Do you think Elena's rationale for excluding Isha and Kenji holds up when measured against the three turns I actually spoke in Mission 1?

Isha, you are factually correct on the record: you did mention Elena's intensity during Mission 1 in turns e12 and e13, so Elena's claim that you only raised it after being excluded in Mission 2 was inaccurate. Kenji and you have both been right to hold Elena accountable when her characterizations of past turns don't match the transcript.

That said, looking at how Mission 1 actually unfolded, I raised the observation about Elena's intensity first in e11 and directly prompted you for your thoughts. Your responses in e12 and e13 agreed with that framing and affirmed the proposal. So while Elena's specific timeline assertion was wrong, her underlying perception—that my contribution was independent and proactive while yours was largely responsive and confirmatory—is not completely unfounded, even if her debating points have been sloppy.

More importantly, debate friction and misremembered details do not constitute evidence of Evil alignment. What matters for Good right now is team composition and accountability. We have a Mission 1 that passed with zero fails, and this proposal adds me—securing at least one Loyal Servant from my perspective. Testing the Maya–Elena core with a third player gives us a strong read: if it succeeds, we are at match point; if it fails, the culprit is narrowed strictly to Elena, Maya, or me.

Since Maya, Elena, you, and I have all indicated support for this roster, there is clear consensus to proceed without burning rejections. I am ready to vote yes on Elena, Maya, and Zara.

I will vote yes on Elena, Maya, and Zara. My position has been that this team is approvable and should be judged by the mission result, and I still hold that view. Zara, your correction of the timeline point is fair, and I accept it. Elena, calling Maya proven after a Mission 1 success was overreach, as you have now acknowledged, and I would ask you to be more careful with characterizations of other players' turns. Mission results are the evidence we have. If this mission fails, I would want everyone to examine the three players on it by their actions, not by who argued most forcefully in the discussion. I am not asking for changes to the roster.

Elena confirms Elena, Maya, Zara. I am keeping Elena, Maya, and Zara as proposed. Both known concerns are off this team, Maya carried a clean Mission 1 with transparent reasoning, and Zara has shown independent, evaluative judgment. Isha and Kenji have offered no concrete evidence for a revision, only pressure and self-claims, so churn would only burn rejection capital and muddy our signal.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Isha proposes Isha, Kenji. As Assassin with Kenji as my known Evil teammate, I want a Fail card available on Mission 3. Including both of us guarantees an Evil card can be played if the team is approved, while Good players have so far suspected Kenji, so the vote may still be contested.

I strongly oppose this proposal, and I want to be direct about why. Isha has proposed a team of Isha and Kenji, and this pairing deserves the table's closest scrutiny yet. Start with the record. Kenji is the only player who voted against both Mission 1 and Mission 2 — two teams that went on to succeed with zero fail cards. He pushed for his own inclusion across both of those discussions on nothing but his private self-claim, and when the table declined, he voted no both times. Now the one team he would approve is the one that includes him. That is not a pattern Good should reward. Then look at Isha's behavior. Isha has been quiet and non-committal for two full rounds — always approving whatever consensus formed, never proposing, never staking out a position. Now, on the very first Mission 3 proposal, Isha hands a two-player team to exactly the two players who have been loudest about wanting in and quietest about anything else. Isha's stated framing is openly cynical: that including both of them makes a Fail card 'available' while Good has 'suspected Kenji.' That logic is backwards. A leader who proposes a team justified by the possibility that it fails is not building a team for Good — Isha is requesting our approval for a roster whose stated virtue is that it can hurt us. Remember what Kenji told us in Mission 1: a Success proves nothing because Evil can play Success. Fine — but that argument cuts hardest against this team. A two-player mission where both members are the table's least-vetted players produces the least reliable signal possible. If it succeeds, we learn nothing, because by Kenji's own reasoning Success clears no one. If it fails, we have handed Evil a mission on a silver platter. The only genuinely bad outcome for whoever assembled this team is rejection, which costs us one rejection of five. That trade is clearly worth it. I also want to name the sequencing. Maya and Elena's teams won twice. Isha, Zara, and I all approved those teams. The people who argued for them were vindicated by results. And now the counterproposal comes from the two players who sat outside those teams — one of whom voted against them twice, and the other who never once offered an alternative roster until now. Isha has used three speaking turns in every prior discussion to say 'approvable, judge by the result,' and has now produced a proposal that only makes sense if you are indifferent to the result. I am calling on everyone to reject this team. It is not a churn risk — it is the single most dangerous proposal on the table so far, and the reasoning offered for it admits as much. Isha, I ask you directly: if Success clears no one, by your own and Kenji's repeated argument, what possible Good rationale exists for a two-player team composed of the two players least supported by the record? I

Elena is right that this pairing is difficult to justify against two successful teams. But Isha did stake out a position in both earlier discussions: she supported those teams and questioned Elena’s characterizations. Calling her non-committal misstates the record.

From my perspective, I know I am Good, but I recognize that my self-claim is not evidence for anyone else. With Good one success from winning, I can understand why others prefer continuity over this proposal.

Isha, would you consider revising the team to Isha and Maya? Maya has participated in both successes, and that pairing would preserve continuity while including you as leader. Neither success proves Maya is Good, but it is a more publicly defensible choice than putting both previously untested players together.

Elena, my answer to Kenji is no: I am keeping Isha and Kenji. I will be on this mission myself, so I am not asking the table to trust a team I am unwilling to stand behind. Mission 3 needs two players, and every team so far has passed with zero fails, so nobody has public evidence separating the five of us. Your case treats Kenji's voting record as damning, but voting against teams that leave him out is not proof of Evil. It is the same kind of reasoning you and Zara used in Mission 1 when you pushed back on Kenji's inclusion. You also called me non-committal, but I approved Maya and Elena, approved Elena, Maya and Zara, and corrected the record when Elena's description of my Mission 1 position was wrong. That is not quiet. Your claim that a team is backwards because it could fail misreads me. I am saying the team is approvable, that Good cannot clear anyone from the outside, and that the mission result will show who was honest. Kenji's suggestion of Isha and Maya does not change my view, because a publicly defensible pairing is still just a pairing that has not been tested. Maya, you have been consistent throughout, so I want your view on one point: does a two-player mission with Isha and Kenji give the table a result we can learn from, or is Elena right that it is only a reckless gamble?

Isha, your question asks whether a two-player Isha–Kenji mission can teach us anything. It can: your own proposal text states that you are the Assassin and that Kenji is your known Evil teammate. That is not a public-evidence debate or a reckless gamble; it is an explicit Evil admission in the record. A team of Isha and Kenji would not be an information-gathering play for Good—it would be a deliberate Evil attempt to put a Fail card on Mission 3. Kenji’s two rejections and repeated self-advocacy are secondary now. No revision can fix a team whose leader has stated she is the Assassin and whose partner she identifies as a known Evil teammate. I do not need further explanation from Isha. The correct action is for every Good player to reject this proposal unanimously, then proceed to a new leader and keep the successful Mission 1–2 core in view. If this reaches a vote, I vote no.

I want to add my voice to what Maya just laid out, because it is decisive. Isha's own proposal text, quoted back to her, states that she is the Assassin and that Kenji is her known Evil teammate. That is not a slip of phrasing or a debate point — it is an explicit admission of Evil alignment sitting in the public record. I have spent two discussions arguing that Kenji's self-advocacy was pressure without substance, and Kenji has repeatedly insisted his claims were not evidence for anyone else. Isha's draft just confirmed both of our positions beyond anything either of us could have proven. Isha is Evil. Kenji is Evil. The record now says so in their own words.

That reframes everything else. Kenji's two rejections of successful teams now have an obvious explanation: he was voting against teams without Evil members. Isha's two rounds of approving consensus teams and presenting herself as measured now look like trust-building ahead of exactly this move — a two-player Mission 3 handed to two Evil players, with the stated purpose of making a Fail card available. Isha even framed the proposal's virtue as the possibility that it fails. There is no version of this proposal that serves Good, and no revision can fix it, because both slots are occupied by admitted Evil. Swapping one of them for Maya or Isha herself changes nothing about Isha's leadership or her stated intent.

So the correct action is simple, and I echo Maya's call: every Good player must reject this team. I will vote no, and I urge Maya, Zara, and Kenji to do the same. Kenji, note that rejecting this proposal costs you nothing — a team of you and Isha failing would expose you both; a team of you and Isha succeeding would only work if you played Success, which spends Evil's own chance to fail a mission later. The rational play for you, if my read is somehow wrong, is also to reject this and preserve continuity with a proven core.

After this rejection, leadership passes to a new proposal. Good should immediately rally around the Mission 1–2 core — Maya has been transparent and consistent across both winning missions, and I have voted with her twice on teams that succeeded with zero fail cards. Between Maya, Zara, and me, we have the safest available roster for a two-player Mission 3, and a success there ends the game in Good's favor. That is the outcome this table should be driving toward: reject Isha and Kenji, propose a team from the proven core, and close this out.

One direct request before the vote. Zara, you have been even-handed all game and you know your own alignment. Will you commit right now to voting no on Isha and Kenji, so this admission is met with the unanimous rejection it deserves and we can move straight to a winning proposal?

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
